title: Why Japan's Overtime Cap Didn't Apply to Doctors Until 2024
hook: Japan capped legal overtime to fight karoshi in 2019 — but let hospital doctors work nearly four times the general limit for another five years.
target_query: why did japan's overtime cap not apply to doctors
free_section_html:
Japan's overtime cap did not apply to hospital doctors until April 2024 because the 2019 law that introduced legal overtime limits, known as the hatarakikata kaikaku (work-style reform) legislation, built in a five-year grace period for physicians, along with construction workers and long-haul truck drivers, on the grounds that these sectors could not absorb the new rules without disrupting essential services.

The 2019 law was Japan's first legally binding cap on overtime, replacing decades of non-binding guidance that employers routinely ignored. For most salaried workers, it set a ceiling of 45 hours of overtime a month and 360 hours a year, with a special exception clause allowing up to 100 hours in a single month and 720 extra hours a year during unavoidable busy periods. Violating these limits can now bring criminal penalties for employers, a first in Japan's postwar labor history.

Doctors, however, were carved out. The government and the Japan Medical Association argued that hospitals, especially in rural areas and in specialties like obstetrics and emergency medicine, depended on younger physicians working extreme hours to keep wards staffed around the clock. Forcing an immediate cap, officials warned, could mean night shifts going uncovered or hospitals closing departments outright. So the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare designed a separate, higher-tier system for physicians that only took effect in April 2024, five years after the general cap started.

Even now, the physician cap is not equal to everyone else's. Doctors at hospitals designated as providing regional emergency or specialized care can be authorized for up to 1,860 hours of overtime a year, roughly two and a half times the extension limit available to ordinary employees, and can legally work overtime equivalent to well over 100 hours in a single busy month. That figure sits uncomfortably close to the threshold Japan's own labor authorities use to recognize a death as karoshi, death from overwork. Understanding why regulators set the bar there, and what happens once a doctor crosses it, requires looking at how Japan actually defines and proves overwork death in the first place.
paid_body_html:
The Two Overtime Ceilings

Japan's 2019 overtime cap did not create one national limit; it created a base limit and a set of negotiated exceptions layered on top. The base rule bars overtime beyond 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year. Employers who need more, because of seasonal demand or a project deadline, can sign a special labor-management agreement allowing up to 100 hours in any single month and 720 extra hours a year, on top of the base allowance, bringing the theoretical annual maximum for a general worker to roughly 960 hours of overtime combined across categories, though sustained use near that ceiling is rare and heavily scrutinized.

Physicians were placed in a separate track altogether. When the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare finally applied caps to doctors in April 2024, it did not simply delay the general rule; it wrote a bespoke framework with four tiers, labeled A, B, C-1 and C-2. Category A, the default for most hospital doctors, caps overtime at 960 hours a year, matching the general worker's outer limit. But categories B and C, reserved for hospitals designated as providing regional emergency care, teaching hospitals training residents, or facilities in areas with chronic doctor shortages, permit up to 1,860 hours of overtime annually. That is not a typo repeated for emphasis; it is roughly double the ceiling that applies to a factory worker or an office clerk under the same national law.

Why Doctors Got a Later, Higher Bar

The justification rests on Japan's uneven distribution of physicians. Tokyo and Osaka have dense concentrations of specialists, while many rural prefectures rely on a small number of doctors rotating through emergency call, outpatient clinics, and inpatient wards at the same hospital. The Japan Medical Association and the health ministry argued during the legislative debate that an immediate, uniform cap would force some hospitals to cut services rather than hire more staff, because there were not enough licensed physicians available to hire in the short term, particularly in obstetrics, emergency medicine, and surgery. The five-year delay before the physician cap took effect was meant to give hospitals time to redistribute shifts, expand task-sharing with nurses, and recruit, though workforce numbers in these specialties have moved slowly.

Construction and trucking received similar multi-year grace periods for comparable reasons: both industries reported labor shortages and warned that immediate caps would disrupt infrastructure projects and supply chains. All three exemptions expired on the same date, April 1, 2024, making it a symbolic deadline in Japanese labor policy, even though the substance of the doctor exemption did not disappear that day. It simply became a formal, numbered category instead of an informal gap in the law.

Karoshi Recognition Runs on a Different Clock

The uncomfortable part of the 1,860-hour ceiling is how it compares to Japan's own definition of overwork death. Since guidelines issued in 2001 by what was then the Ministry of Health and Welfare, Japanese labor standards inspection offices have used two thresholds to decide whether a death or serious illness qualifies for workers' compensation as karoshi: overtime exceeding roughly 100 hours in the month before the event, or an average exceeding roughly 80 hours a month over the preceding two to six months. These are not medical diagnoses; they are administrative triggers that shift the burden of proof, making it easier for a bereaved family to win compensation without having to independently prove that overwork caused a stroke, heart attack, or suicide.

A doctor working near the top of the Category B or C allowance, spread evenly across a year, would be logging overtime close to or above that 80-hour monthly average almost continuously. Labor lawyers and some physician advocacy groups have pointed out this arithmetic since the framework was drafted: the government set a legal ceiling for one profession that sits inside the zone its own compensation system treats as evidence of life-threatening overwork for everyone else. The health ministry's position is that the ceiling is an outer limit meant to be reduced over time through workforce reform, not a target, and that most physicians work below it. Hospital-level surveys conducted before the cap took effect suggested a meaningful minority of hospital-based doctors, particularly residents and those in emergency and obstetric departments, were already logging overtime in that range before any legal cap existed.

What Changes After 2024 — and What Doesn't

The practical enforcement mechanism is a certification system: hospitals wanting to use the higher B or C allowances must apply for designation, document staffing shortages, and commit to measures like mandatory rest periods after long shifts and interval rules between the end of one shift and the start of the next. Labor standards inspection offices can audit hospitals and, in theory, revoke designations, though the health ministry has published only limited public data on how many hospitals have actually lost a designation since 2024.

Cases involving young doctors and karoshi have appeared in Japanese labor tribunals and press coverage over the past two decades, usually involving residents or newly qualified physicians in high-acuity departments logging overtime far beyond even the newly legal ceiling. These cases predate the 2024 framework and helped drive the political pressure to regulate physician hours at all; critics argue the resulting 1,860-hour ceiling formalizes a level of risk the health ministry's own compensation guidelines already flag as dangerous, rather than eliminating it. The framework includes a stated intention to lower the ceiling over subsequent years as hospitals restructure staffing, but no binding date has been set for when Category B and C hospitals must fall to the same 960-hour limit as everyone else. For now, the profession most equipped to treat the consequences of overwork remains the one legally permitted to work the most of it.
key_takeaways: Japan's 2019 overtime cap set a general limit of 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year, with an exception allowing up to 100 hours a month and 720 extra hours a year.
Doctors, along with construction and trucking, received a five-year exemption from the cap that only ended in April 2024.

Even under the new physician-specific framework, hospitals designated for emergency or specialized care can authorize up to 1,860 hours of annual overtime, roughly double the general worker's outer limit.

Japan's karoshi (overwork death) compensation guidelines use roughly 80 to 100 hours of monthly overtime as the threshold for presuming a work-related cause, a range the legal physician ceiling overlaps with.
No binding date exists for lowering the higher physician overtime ceilings to match the general worker limit.
